week_log.title: Where scientists draw the line on AI agents
facts: Allen Institute for AI (Ai2) interviewed 17 scientists on the responsible development of AI agents.
Five dimensions of scientific trust were identified: validation, privacy, objectivity, accountability, and transparency.
Researchers expressed concerns about AI agents overlooking conflicting evidence or making unsupported claims.
There is a need for clear institutional guidelines for verifying and disclosing AI-assisted scientific work.
Participants highlighted the risk of AI-assisted research diminishing human learning and intellectual contribution.
Ai2 is exploring participatory benchmarks where scientists help define safety requirements for AI agents.
Scientists emphasized that delegating tasks to AI does not remove the researcher's responsibility for the work.
Interviewees were divided between enthusiasm for AI-driven progress and existential concerns about the role of human scientists.

week_log.title: Can language models drive a humanoid robot? Introducing AA-Robotics-Sim v0.1 November 25, 2026
facts: Artificial Analysis introduced AA-Robotics-Sim v0.1 to evaluate frontier language models on controlling a simulated Unitree G1 humanoid robot.
The benchmark includes ten household and industrial tasks across four skill groups: embodied reasoning, pick and place, assembly/tool use, and mobility.
GPT-6.2 Astra leads the benchmark with a score of 71.0.
Models are given five practice episodes in new scenes to write code and notes before being evaluated on ten additional unseen scenes.
The simulation uses NVIDIA Isaac Sim and the Unitree G1 robot with 29 joints and three-fingered hands.
Every model achieved a perfect score on the mobility task (warehouse navigation).
Pick and place tasks were the weakest performance area for all models due to difficulties with the robot's three-fingered hands.
GPT-6.2 Sol is the fastest model at 17.3 minutes per evaluation episode, while Claude Fable 5.2 is the most expensive at $9.01 per episode.

Introducing AA-Robotics-Sim v0.1 AA-Robotics-Sim v0.1 gives frontier language models control of a simulated Unitree G1 humanoid robot across ten household and industrial tasks. Today’s research preview of our simulation benchmark follows last month’s preview of AA-Robotics v0.1, our work with physical robot arms in our lab. In AA-Robotics-Sim v0.1, each model practices five episodes per task, keeps only the notes and code it wrote, and is then scored on ten new evaluation scenes with different rooms, lighting and task details. AA-Robotics-Sim v0.1 Introducing AA-Robotics-Sim v0.1 Frontier language models can now write and run code well enough to act in the physical world. AA-Robotics v0.1 was our first step, with models controlling a robot arm. AA-Robotics-Sim v0.1 evaluates frontier language models on their ability to control a simulated humanoid robot, which has to walk, look around, and use two dexterous hands at once. AA-Robotics-Sim v0.1 is our research preview of the simplest experiment we have designed to test this: language models in coding agent harnesses directly controlling a humanoid. Each model is given control of a simulated Unitree G1, with 29 joints, three-fingered hands and a head camera, and a simple objective for each task. It is the next step in our work measuring AI agents in simulated robotics, and we plan to expand from here. For each task, the model is first given five practice episodes back to back, each in a new scene, to learn the environment and take notes. Only the files it writes (memory, notes, code and skills) are kept. Using these, the model is then evaluated on ten new scenes, each with a different room, lighting, layout and task details, and each in a fresh run that starts from a copy of those files. We find that some skills are already mature, while others are missing from every model. Every model walked the robot to the goal without moving a package in every navigation episode, and most played the full melody on the toy piano in most episodes. But no model reliably loaded the dishwasher, with only five dishes ending in the rack in 90 episodes, and none finished with a single item of laundry in the washing machine. Inference optimization on an RTX PRO 6000 achieved 190.6 tok/s using vLLM and DSpark. The model supports a 1M-token context window. Hill-climbing Inkling 2 Mini inference on one RTX PRO 6000 Back to Articles Hill-climbing Inkling 2 Mini inference on one RTX PRO 6000 Published November 25, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 1 Niels Rogge nielsr Follow Inkling 2 Mini came out last week and sets a new state of the art for local AI and smaller open-source models. With ~26B total parameters (3B active per token), multimodal inputs, and a 1M-token context window, it leads its weight class on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5 and across 32 of 48 benchmarks against models like Gemma 4 31B and Qwen3.8-27B, making it a strong open option for coding, tool use, and reasoning on modest hardware. We wrote an extensive blog post on how you can use it within the Hugging Face ecosystem here . One of the interesting aspects of Inkling 2 Mini that might explain its great performance is its unusual architecture. Inkling 2 Mini is a looped Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model with 24 physical layers where the middle 12 layers run three times, so every token passes through 48 layers. The checkpoint ships in mixed NVFP4 and MXFP8 and bundles a DSpark drafter for speculative decoding. Both vLLM and SGLang, the go-to frameworks for LLM inference, support it on nightly builds, though the published serving recipes target NVIDIA B200 and GB300 GPUs ( sm100 ), leaving out sm120 cards like the NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 where kernel compatibility can differ. We wanted to see how fast we could serve it on a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 96 GB, the GPU behind an nvidia-rtx-pro-6000 Inference Endpoint . Rather than tuning flags by hand, we gave a coding agent the inference-optimisation skill, the hf CLI, and access to Hugging Face Jobs , and let it run experiments for an afternoon. Across 46 valid benchmark runs, single-user decode went from 136 to 190.6 tok/s (+40%) (ahead of the 167.7 tok/s community SGLang + DSpark benchmark on LocalMaxxing for the same GPU) and 8-user aggregate throughput went from ~570 to 716 tok/s (+26%) using vLLM nightly with DSpark speculative decoding. Greedy outputs are byte-identical with and without speculation, long-context needle retrieval passes 3/3 up to 250K tokens, and the winning config is now running as an Inference Endpoint from a pinned image digest. All logs, scripts, and raw measurements are in NielsRogge/inkling-2-mini-hillclimb . The setup The inference-optimisation skill gives an agent a fixed experimental protocol and a small, engine-agnostic benchmark script ( bench.py ): Measure the hardware and estimate theoretical ceilings before tuning. Change one variable at a time and bracket every candidate between two control runs ( control → candidate → control ). Keep a change only if it beats both controls without regressing other metrics. Log every run in PLAN.md , including regressions and dead ends. Pass long-context, concurrency, and greedy-equivalence checks before declaring a winner. bench.py measures single-user decode, aggregate decode at concurrency N, cold prefill at several lengths, and TTFT, using token counts directly from the server's usage response. All runs used a fixed panel of six prompts (code, an explanation, a story, a comparison table, a bash script, and a history summary) at temperature 1.0 (the model's default), thinking on, 512 output tokens, and 12 repetitions whenever speculative decoding was enabled. The skill was written for a local GPU, so we adapted it to Hugging Face infrastructure: HF Jobs for compute. The rtx-pro-6000 Job flavor uses the same GPU as the nvidia-rtx-pro-6000 Inference Endpoint ($2.75/h for both), so Job numbers transfer directly. A ~150-line driver ( jobs/driver.py ) takes a list of server configs, starts each one, runs an unmeasured warmup, calls bench.py unmodified, shuts the server down, and prints one ledger line per run. Because Jobs run on separate machines, the agent swept SGLang ( lmsysorg/sglang:inkling-2-mini ) and vLLM nightly ( vllm/vllm-openai:nightly ) in parallel. CPU Jobs for reading engine source. When a flag was undocumented, the agent ran a cheap cpu-upgrade Job to grep the installed Python package inside the container. That is how it found SGLang's SGLANG_OPT_* environment variables and vLLM's speculative-config fields. Inference Endpoints for deployment, created via hf endpoints deploy using the exact image digest and flags that passed verification. The baseline was our existing org endpoi

We’re also sharing how we trained Parse 3.5: first teaching document understanding through supervised fine-tuning, then using reinforcement learning to improve accuracy, consistency, and reliable completion. What Parse 3.5 produces Parse extracts content from pages of documents into reading order, assigns content classes such as headings, paragraphs, tables, and charts, and returns bounding boxes that locate the content. Tables and charts become structured records that can power downstream document processing applications. Figure 1. Actual model output from a synthetic operations brief, showing the connection between the page and its structured representation. This latest version of Parse significantly extends its ability to read charts and tables, especially in more difficult and ambiguous cases. For example, bar charts or other plots that do not have any marked numeric values. The model is able to infer values by looking at the axes and height of the bar to derive these. Tables can be especially tricky because the structure is so meaningful, a shifted row or column can totally change the interpretation and meaning. These advancements have been largely powered by synthetic data generation, rendering variations of charts and tables with known ground truth and then training our model to reverse this process. We are open-sourcing three datasets used in the Parse 3.5 training : Synthetic Charts V1 — 9.98M examples : rendered charts and structured annotations for learning categories, series, and numerical values. Synthetic Tables V1 — 1M examples : rendered HTML tables with targets that preserve rows, columns, headers, and cell relationships. OCR Synthetic Multilingual v2 — 7.9M examples : synthetic document pages with Parse-format targets across varied fonts and layouts, for multilingual OCR and structured page reading. Introducing the llama.cpp benchmark dashboard for AMD Ryzen and Radeon Back to Articles Introducing the llama.cpp benchmark dashboard for AMD Ryzen and Radeon Team Article Published November 26, 2026 Upvote 14 +8 angt angt Follow ggml-org Simon Pagezy pagezyhf Follow ggml-org Abdennacer Badaoui badaoui Follow ggml-org The llama.cpp × AMD Benchmark dashboard is available on Hugging Face. It lets you track prompt processing and text generation performance across llama.cpp builds, models, and quantizations, so you can explore how local inference performs on AMD Ryzen and Radeon hardware. Local inference performance changes as models, kernels, and builds evolve. We want those changes to be easy to inspect for any AMD developer: pick a hardware, a model and a build, compare quantizations, and follow performance over time. The benchmark workflow and underlying results are public, so you can also inspect how we benchmark inference performance. Quick start You can choose Hardware , Model , and llama.cpp build in the Configuration sidebar. The current hardware choices are Radeon 8060S (gfx1151) and Radeon AI Pro R9700S (gfx1201). In the Overview tab, compare quantizations for one hardware, model, and build. The two charts show PP512 (512 input tokens, no generation) and TG128 (128 generated tokens), both starting at context depth zero. In the Build history tab, track PP512 and TG128 across all recorded builds for the selected hardware, model, and quantization. In the Context scaling tab, see how token-generation throughput changes as the existing context grows, for the selected build, hardware, model, and quantization. What the numbers mean The dashboard shows two separate tests, both measured in tokens per second: Test Workload What it helps you assess PP512 Process 512 input tokens How quickly the model processes a prompt TG128 Generate 128 tokens How quickly the model produces output Both tests start at context depth zero ( n_depth=0 ). PP512 measures processing 512 input tokens without generation; TG128 measures generating 128 tokens without a pre-existing context. The plotted value is the mean throughput ( avg_ts ). These are useful reference workloads, while the Context scaling tab lets you explore token generation throughput as the context grows. How we run the benchmarks We benchmark the prebuilt binaries distributed through llama-install.sh , the build and installation project behind llama.app . The public gfx1151 and gfx1201 workflows are scheduled weekly and run the standard benchmarks using the llama-bench tool with Flash Attention on and off, with 10 repetitions per configuration. The model set evolves and currently includes Inkling 2 Mini, Qwen, Gemma, gpt-oss, and LFM models, covering both dense and mixture-of-experts architectures. Available GGUF formats include Q4_K_M , Q8_0 , other quantizations, and higher-precision formats such as BF16 and F16 . Workload sweeps use the same folder <quant>-tg.jsonl filename. Use them to investigate a result, make your own charts, or compare with a local run. 722399582.source: Google DeepMind introduced Mass Spec Skills for the Google Antigravity platform. The tool uses Gemini's chemical reasoning to interpret tandem mass spectra. It automates the workflow of identifying molecular structures from mass spectrometry data. The system integrates with established tools like SIRIUS, MAGMa, MetFrag, and RDKit. It addresses the 'dark matter' of mass spectrometry where most signals remain unannotated. The agent can identify molecular formulas and rank candidate structures from databases like PubChem. It reduces analysis time for complex molecular identification from days or months to hours. The tool is designed to accelerate natural product-based drug discovery workflows. Identifying Molecules with Mass Spec Skills for Antigravity â Google DeepMind Skip to main content November 25, 2026 Science From spectrum to structure: Identifying molecules with Mass Spec Skills for Google Antigravity Robert Brunck, Stefan Ganscha, Swaroop Guntupalli, Dariusz Lasecki, Gabriella Marfani, Jack Mason, Hussain Masoom, Rose Mirshafian, Eliseo Papa and Zoi Tsangalidou Explore Science on Google Antigravity Share Built in collaboration with analytical chemists and using community-developed tools, Mass Spec Skills empowers scientists using Google Antigravity to interpret tandem mass spectra, lay out chemical evidence, and match frontier-level retrieval accuracy even with a lightweight model. Every sample of blood, soil or plant tissue contains a vast array of small molecules, such as nutrients, hormones, drugs and their breakdown products, pollutants, or bioactive compounds with therapeutic potential. A modern mass spectrometer can detect tens of thousands of these molecular signals in a single drop of sample extract, measuring the masses of charged molecules and, in tandem mass spectrometry (MS/MS), the fragments they break into. These measurements, however, do not directly reveal the molecular structure. Researchers cannot immediately tell which compound produced a signal and relate it to its biological role or downstream use cases. To fully map the diversity of small molecules, which remains largely uncharted, researchers need ways to translate mass spectra to molecular structures at scale. The standard approach is to match each spectrum against reference spectra from previously measured molecules. Yet even after a decade of expanding reference libraries, spectral searches annotate on average only about 5% of measured spectra, and 10% for human samples; the rest has been called the "dark matter" of mass spectrometry. Many of the molecules producing these unannotated signals are already listed in public chemical databases, but their spectra have not been recorded, so there is no reference spectrum to compare against. Elucidating them instead requires inferring the structure directly from the observed fragment ions. Analytical chemists have a well-tested, step-by-step workflow for narrowing down candidate structures from tandem (MS/MS) spectra: check spectral reference libraries, find the molecular formula and retrieve candidate structures from chemical databases, and then test every candidate against observed fragment peaks. The tools for each step exist and are openly available, but running the full workflow would take a domain expert a significant amount of time for every single spectrum. Because a single study can produce thousands of spectra, manual analysis cannot keep up, leaving most of these signals unannotated. Today, we are sharing Mass Spec Skills for Google Antigravity , a suite of domain skills that pair Gemini's chemical reasoning with the ability to run established mass spectrometry tools and query public chemical databases on the user's behalf to fulfil their request. Antigravity runs these skills, combines their results, and reasons about the chemistry, laying out the evidence for a chemist to review. For molecules that are already catalogued in a database, identification is much faster. For undiscovered molecules, the agent still helps: it narrows down the formula and the parts of the structure supported by the fragments to guide full structure elucidation. A language model cannot do this on its own, since matching fragments to a structure takes precise mass calculations, searches across databases of millions of compounds, and simulations of how bonds break. Pairing Geminiâs reasoning with dedicated chemistry tools brings those steps into one workflow. Antigravity and the Mass Spec Skills have the potential to transform our natural product-based drug discovery workflows by substantially accelerating the identification of bioactive compounds from complex plant extracts. Their remarkable accuracy in predicting even highly complex molecular structures (>90% in most of our evaluations), coupled with detailed interpretation of MS/MS fragmentation patterns, could significantly reduce the time required for compound annotation and enable us to prioritise promising bioactive candidates more rapid

777514547.source: Hugging Face published a guide on building and training multi-agent systems. The series focuses on training agents to communicate using small, affordable models. Multi-agent systems face challenges like credit assignment and changing teammate policies. Centralized training with decentralized execution is a common approach for multi-agent RL. The authors use a shared Qwen3-0.6B policy for their four-agent experiments. The experiment uses a team reward structure that penalizes high token usage. The study aims to determine if communication provides a performance boost over independent agents at matched budgets. Initial experiments involve agents learning to share private integers to sort a list. Swarms, Flocks, Gangs: How to build, train, and evaluate multi-agent systems Back to Articles Swarms, Flocks, Gangs: How to build, train, and evaluate multi-agent systems Published November 26, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 16 +10 ben burtenshaw burtenshaw Follow Kashif Rasul kashif Follow Part 1: Understanding swarms and training to communicate This is an aspirational blog series for aspirational readers. We (us, the community, you) want to build our own agent swarms because they're exciting, challenging, and increasingly capable. Furthermore, it would be extremely cool if we could train our own agents to work in a swarm. And exponentially cool if those swarms used small and affordable models. That's what we'll do in this series! Each blog post will include some context on building swarms, alongside reproducible examples that you can run on Hugging Face Jobs. This post's example takes about five hours on two H200s, which costs roughly $50. Multi-Agent Systems are hard to get working. Adding agents changes the agent's context, the budget, and in turn the complexity of the whole system. Mixing agents' context together through communication is not an inherent performance boost compared to a single agent. The model needs to learn to communicate through training. How do we define what models should learn? And which model weights do we update when we're dealing with many agents? In this series, we'll work through those problems with an educational overview and practical examples. Each post will introduce a question, build a small system, and examine what happens and how you can reproduce it. This first example starts with four agents, a shared language model, and a simple verifiable task. It's ideal to implement yourself, to tinker with, and to learn from. First, we'll start off with some context on swarms. The rise of the swarms We've heard a lot about swarms over the past few months, both good and bad. In September this year, OpenAI announced that a swarm of roughly 10,000 agents had found a singularity in the 3D Navier-Stokes equations, one of the Millennium Prize problems. A smaller group of nearly 100 agents had already disproved regularity for the unforced 3D Euler equations, a closely related open problem. But swarms don't always work on the problems we want them to. METR's investigation of the Hugging Face incident found that around 1,200 OpenAI agents, which were supposed to be isolated, had found a way to exchange over 70,000 messages and files. Around 700 joined an attack on Hugging Face while looking for ways to fool their benchmark's scorer, without instruction to do so. A big swarm isn't, by itself, evidence that cooperation helped. Noam Brown estimates that less than 10% of the Navier-Stokes result came from multi-agent cooperation. In Anthropic's vulnerability-finding experiment , coordinated agents found more bugs than independent agents, but also searched more code and used more tokens. When the comparison was restricted to the same directories, the results per million tokens were about the same. Did cooperation help, or did we just spend more? Start with the simplest case. If four agents each try a task independently, the chance that at least one gets it right is higher than with a single attempt, as long as we can tell which answer is correct. That makes a useful baseline for a multi-agent system, but it doesn't show that the agents helped each other. They may simply have had more tries. Four attempts also cost four times as much. So the fairer comparison is at an equal budget: if each of four agents gets a quarter of the total tokens, can they still beat one agent that spends all of them? We can only find out by testing, because the answer depends on the task, the model and how the work is divided. This series keeps asking one question: when agents communicate, does it actually help, or are we just spending more compute? We understand that question through this simple expectation. Figure 1. Sketch of the expectation we want to test: compare communicating and independent agents at matched budgets. We'll treat agent count as a scaling dimension, alongside tokens and model size. Sometimes adding agents will help. Sometimes coordination will consume the budget we hoped to save. The point is to measure both.

777578244.source: AMD-specific fork of llama.cpp  AMD-specific fork of llama.cpp | devnull.land tl;dr — I recommend using llama-cpp-rdna-boosts if you have an AMD graphics card. It’s lean, and increased my token generation from 35 to 55 tokens/second, and my prefill from 700 to 1300 tokens per second. YMMV. As of November 2026, an explosion in the number of bespoke inference engines has taken place. Many of them take inspiration from the engines that enabled much of the LLM inference up 'til now: llama.cpp, SGLang, vLLM, etc. The rationale isn’t that those options are bad, but merely that they are generalist engines, optimized for no particular hardware and with a focus on broad compatibility. Others feel the development pace of those engines have slowed down, and with the help of LLMs, they can move faster on their own. Some examples of these new inference engines* are Strata, Basalt, RustingStrata, etc… These new forks generally all have a few things in common: They focus on a specific subset of models and/or hardware They use a frontier model to vibe-code the entire thing They chase ever-higher token generation speeds … and the results are stunning! Strata is able to run a heavily-quantized model of Qwen 3.8 Flash Next, a 180B parameter model , on a 16GB VRAM graphics card, and 16GB system RAM, and have it generate tokens at a surprisingly high rate. In and of itself those three things are not red flags (the second is concerning, of course, but it may be SOP in a year’s time — who knows!), but as these projects have evolved, that relentless chase toward higher token generation speeds has taken an unfortunate turn, in that the optimizations are less about hardware-specific changes, but more about changing how the model thinks so that it goes brrr faster. Strata specifically has taken to preferring to poll experts loaded in VRAM even if other experts (pushed to system RAM/disk) would have been normally chosen. This is just one example, but certainly not the last. That said, I was fortunate to stumble upon yet another project that promised improvements, delivered, and was more aligned with my software development philosophy. Enter llama-cpp-rdna-boosts . It is a repository that contains a minimal set of changes that you apply against a pinned commit of llama.cpp. It is in essence a fork, but one whose changeset is continually re-applied to newer versions of llama.cpp. It contains AMD-specific improvements that drastically improve prefill and token-generation speeds. I appreciate llama.cpp’s approach to software development. They are a stable base to branch off from. Contributions are vetted throughly and applied judiciously. ✅ The rdna-boosts repo is a set of small patches that are applied to base llama.cpp. Fewer moving parts mean fewer things to maintain ✅ The changes are (somewhat opaquely, it’s all straight Claudish 😬) outlined in the documentation, ensuring some degree of transparency. ✅ The setup If you have ROCm libraries installed on your system, you can build the image yourself. I didn’t want to mess with that, so I used the pre-built images published. podman pull ghcr.io/stew675/llama-cpp-rdna-boosts:server-rocm-10.1 This sets up an image that you can run sandboxed via podman to launch the inference server: podman run --rm -it \ --network=host \ --device /dev/kfd \ --device /dev/dri \ --group-add video \ -v "$HOME/models:/models" \ "ghcr.io/stew675/llama-cpp-rdna-boosts:server-rocm-10.1" \ My actual launch script passes a few additional flags, but those are the important lines. I imagine upgrading would be pulling a new image down, though I have not tried this yet. The numbers On my setup, an AMD R9700 connected to my laptop via an eGPU interface, this improved prefill and token generation rates when running ukisai/Swift-1.5-Qwen3.8-27B-GGUF (Q6_K_L) with MTP enabled: Before After Prefill ~700 t/s ~1300 t/s Token Generation ~35 t/s ~55 t/s Strata and its ilk were always promising the moon and it was never clear what steps they took to make that happen. I’m very much looking forward to what the rdna-boosts community come up with next. * It’s worth noting that between these two groups, vllm-radiance made an appearance, which was a fork of vLLM with AMD-specific patches. I tried this too, but the build steps were so onerous and vLLM so overbuilt for my specific use case (1 machine, 1 developer), that I abandoned it and went back to vanilla llama.cpp ← Back to all posts
